claim: Decoding an instruction-tuned language model under a context-free grammar, within a finite token budget, can guarantee that what comes back is actually accepted by the grammar, rather than only guaranteeing that each prefix could in principle still be completed, and can improve the quality of the structures produced at the same time. The validity bar is that 100% of returned outputs are accepted by the target grammar, with nothing invalid or truncated returned whenever an accepted completion can be certified inside the available budget. The quality bar is that task-specific correctness exceeds that of the strongest applicable earlier constrained decoder, using the same base model and the same token budget.

experiments: Fix the shared protocol. Setup: three instruction-tuned models of 3B to 8B on three tasks: 100 schema-constrained JSON examples, the 1,034-example validation split of a text-to-SQL benchmark, and 6,185 temporal-logic formulas, all at a uniform budget of 120 tokens. Measured per task: syntactic acceptance, a task correctness measure (schema validity, execution accuracy, or equivalence of the resulting automaton to the gold formula), perplexity, and seconds per output. An unconstrained baseline samples 10 generations at temperature 0.8; a sample-and-filter baseline reuses those 10, discards invalid ones and picks a survivor at random per seed. Stochastic baselines report mean and spread over seeds, deterministic ones a single run. One L40S GPU throughout.

Completed-output validity and schema correctness on JSON. Setup: run the method with its two settings fixed and compare against seven alternatives including three widely used constrained-generation engines, at the shared 120-token budget. Result: 100.0% syntactically valid and 100.0% schema-valid on all three models. The best alternative reaches 90.0%, 90.0% and 89.0% schema validity on the three models, so none of them closes the gap. Decoding takes 3.5 to 4.1 seconds per output with perplexity 1.11 to 1.14.

Does the guarantee survive on a harder grammar while improving executable output? Setup: the SQL validation split, beam width 4, the lookahead weight tuned per model. Result: 100.0% syntactic correctness on every model, with execution accuracy 61.1%, 51.5% and 62.8%. The best alternative per model reaches 59.2%, 49.4% and 61.5%, so the margins are 1.3 to 1.9 points, the narrowest of the three tasks. Decoding costs 6.3 to 13.0 seconds per output.

Does it extend to temporal logic and semantic, not just syntactic, correctness? Setup: the 6,185-formula set, beam width 4, weight tuned per model, against the unconstrained, sample-and-filter and one constrained baseline. Result: 100.0% syntactic correctness and 29.6%, 22.1% and 31.6% equivalence to the gold formula, against the best alternative's 24.4%, 15.2% and 31.0%. On the third model the margin is 0.6 points, essentially a tie; the comparison method is at 99.9-100.0% syntactic correctness, so the validity gap is negligible here.

Do the other decoders fail on JSON only because 120 tokens is too few? Setup: repeat the JSON comparison for four alternatives at budgets of 512, 1,024, 2,048 and 4,096 tokens instead of 120. Result: their schema validity is essentially flat across budgets, staying at 90%, 85% and 91% for one engine, 91-93% for another, 79-83% for a third, and 89.8-92.9% for a fourth. No method reaches 100% schema validity at any enlarged budget, while one engine's time rises from 13.3 to 113.8 seconds. So the shortfall is structural, not a budget artefact.
